To bully someone means to repeatedly use your power or strength to frighten, hurt, or control a person who is weaker than you — or who cannot easily fight back.

The key word here is power. A bully always has some kind of advantage over the victim. That advantage could be physical strength, popularity, numbers (a group against one person), age, authority, or even money. The bully uses that advantage as a weapon.
What Makes Something "Bullying" and Not Just a Fight?

Three things must be true for an action to count as bullying:

1. There is a power imbalance.
The person doing it is stronger, more powerful, or more influential in some way. It is not a fair situation. The victim feels unable to defend themselves properly.

2. It happens repeatedly.
Bullying is not a single, one-time argument or conflict. It is a pattern. The same person keeps targeting the same victim, again and again. This is what makes it so damaging — it traps the victim in a cycle they cannot escape.

3. The intent is to harm, control, or dominate.
The bully is not making a mistake. They are doing it on purpose — to cause pain, to show power, or to force the victim to do something.

If even one of these three is missing, it might be a conflict or a dispute, but it may not technically be "bullying."
How Does Bullying Happen? (Its Many Forms)

Bullying is not always physical. It can take many shapes:

Physical bullying — hitting, pushing, shoving, or damaging someone's belongings. This is the most visible form.

Verbal bullying — name-calling, insulting, mocking, making cruel jokes, or threatening someone with words. It is invisible to others but deeply harmful.

Social bullying (also called relational bullying) — intentionally leaving someone out of a group, spreading rumors about them, turning friends against them, or humiliating them in front of others. This attacks a person's reputation and relationships.

Cyberbullying — bullying that happens online, through social media, text messages, or apps. It is particularly harmful because it can reach the victim anywhere, even at home, and the audience can be enormous.

All of these are forms of the verb to bully. A person can bully using any of these methods.
A Special Pattern: "Bully Someone Into Doing Something"

This is a very important and common way the verb is used. When you bully someone into doing something, you are using threats, fear, or pressure to force them to do it against their will.

Think of it as: "I will keep making your life terrible until you do what I want."

Examples:

  • "The older students bullied the younger ones into handing over their lunch money." (They used fear to force them to give money.)
  • "He was bullied into staying quiet about what he saw." (Fear made him stay silent.)
  • "The aggressive manager bullied his team into working overtime every weekend." (He used his authority and intimidation to force them.)

In this pattern, the victim does the action — but only because they are afraid. It is not a free choice. This is what makes it bullying, not persuasion.
Example Sentences (to See the Verb in Action)

• "She was bullied every day at school because she was new and quiet."
  • "A group of boys bullied him for years before a teacher finally noticed."
  • "Just because someone is bigger or louder does not give them the right to bully others."
  • "He bullied his way through the company, stepping on everyone around him to get to the top."
  • "She refused to be bullied into changing her decision."

Notice how in the last two examples, "bully" carries a sense of using force or intimidation to get an outcome — not just in schools, but in adult life too.

An important thing to understand is that "to bully" is not just a school-yard word. It applies to many real-life situations:

  • At school — the most commonly thought of context. Older or stronger students targeting weaker or younger ones.
  • At work — a boss or colleague who repeatedly humiliates, threatens, or undermines someone. This is often called workplace bullying.
  • At home — a family member who controls or intimidates another through fear.
  • Online — through social media, gaming, or messaging platforms.
  • Between nations or groups — in political or international contexts, a powerful nation or group that uses threats or force to control a weaker one is sometimes described as bullying.

The verb works across all these contexts without changing its core meaning.

These words are close in meaning to bully but have slight differences in intensity or focus:

  • Intimidate — to make someone feel afraid so they do what you want. Less ongoing than bullying.
  • Harass — to trouble or disturb someone persistently. Can be less physically threatening than bullying.
  • Torment — to cause someone great pain or suffering, often repeatedly. Stronger emotional weight.
  • Coerce — to force someone to do something using threats. Very similar to "bully into."
  • Browbeat — to frighten someone with your aggressive manner or words. Often used in arguments or debates.
  • Victimize — to treat someone unfairly and make them a target repeatedly.

It is not the same as teasing. Friendly teasing between equals who both find it funny is not bullying. Bullying causes real fear or pain and is not a mutual joke.

It is not the same as discipline. A teacher or parent setting firm rules is not bullying, even if the child dislikes it. Bullying requires the intention to harm and the absence of a legitimate reason.

It is not the same as a single argument or conflict. Two people having a heated disagreement or even one bad confrontation does not make one of them a bully. Bullying is a repeated, one-sided pattern.

It is not always loud or obvious. Bullying can be quiet and subtle — a whisper campaign, silent exclusion, or a small but consistent act of humiliation. The damage it does is no less real.
The Emotional Core of the Word

When you use the verb to bully, you are describing an action that is fundamentally about abuse of power. To bully is to make someone feel small, afraid, and helpless — and to do it deliberately, over time, because you can. That is what gives the word its weight and its moral judgment. When you say someone is being bullied, you are not just describing what is happening — you are saying that it is wrong.
